newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina seen in struggle to meet IMF targets.
newsitem.headline: Argentina seen in struggle to meet IMF targets.

text.p: Despite an austere fiscal package approved late last year and steady economic growth, Argentina will barely meet first-half fiscal targets agreed with the International Monetary Fund, economists said.

Amid expectations that Argentina will have great difficulty in achieving its yearly deficit goal of $3.0 billion, the government is already trying to secure a new extended fund facility agreement with the IMF for 1998-2000.
"It's best to negotiate when you can still balance your books," said Jose Luis Espert, director of the economic think tank Econometrica.
Analysts said the first-quarter fiscal deficit would reach about $1.04 billion, in line with targets, even though tax collection are expected fall short of expectations.

"First-quarter collection will not reach the targets agreed with the IMF, but spending will also drop, meaning they will average out and the agreement will be met," Tax Policy Undersecretary Guillermo Rodriguez Use said on Tuesday.
He estimated collection during the rest of the year would average $3.8 million a month, or 10 percent more than in 1997.

The government expects to meet its second-quarter deficit goal of $360 million through strict spending controls and with estimated rises in the collection of income taxes (30.5 percent), personal wealth taxes (45.8 percent) and petrol taxes (87.5 percent).

The think tank Macroeconomica in a report said the government would likely meet targets for collecting taxes on petrol and personal wealth. But it said income tax targets would be more difficult to reach, even though the huge Argentine oil company YPF will pay income tax of about $200 million for the first time since it was privatized in 1993.
"Even if income tax is slightly less than forecast, value-added tax should grow more than the stipulated eight percent," Macroeconomica said in a study.
"There's a good chance Argentina will meet its targets, although there's little room to maneuver with spending if there's any fall in collections, which should be monitored closely," it said.
Jose Rutman, an economist at consultancy Broda y Asociados, said, "The odds are tough but possible....If there's a gap, it will be very small."
"Second-quarter collection will rise a lot, at least by two digits. It won't be easy, but you usually have high revenues and low expenses in that period, so it's possible," he said.
